name: Tomas Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the farm manager at Eastfield Community Farm, which is owned by about 600 local members as a cooperative. We milk 120 cows on grass, grow six acres of vegetables and run a farm shop. My day starts at five with the milking, then I check the grass growth figures the satellite app sends overnight and let the AI plan which paddock the cows go to next. After that it's the volunteers, the vegetable team and, most afternoons, a meeting with the board.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best is the cows on fresh grass in May, and the kids from the village school coming to see a calf born. Worst is the pay, frankly, because a co-op farm pays what members vote for, and that's less than a commercial manager gets. Ines teaches part-time, we have a mortgage on a terrace in Brockton, two kids, and about two weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shame, honestly. I was hoping for more than a better search engine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I was a bit disappointed, because I use it every day and it does help with grazing plans and the board papers. I'd post that it's still worth having, just not the miracle anyone promised. I'd keep showing other farmers what it does well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe, and so is my pay, low as it is. Nothing gets easier on money either. The cows still need milking at five, the mortgage still goes out on the first, and we're still two weeks from overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the grazing app and the AI for the rota and the board reports, and maybe try it on the shop's stock orders. I'd ask the board for a small pay rise in the spring budget, with the hours I've saved as my argument. And I'd keep teaching the volunteers to use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly let down. Fine, really, apart from the usual money squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it actually save you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hours a week, mostly writing the board report and working out the milking rota around volunteers' holidays. I used to do that on Sunday nights. Now I read the kids a story instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the board give you that rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two percent, because they've got a heating bill on the shop and a hundred other things. The members love the farm but they're careful with money. I'd take it and say thank you.

say: I'd say I'm **disappointed**, because the AI I use daily helps but isn't a miracle.
I'd keep showing other farmers what the tools **do well**.
think: I think my **job and pay** stay safe, low as the pay is.
We're still **two weeks** from the overdraft, and that doesn't change.
do: Keep using the **grazing app** and AI for the rota and board reports.
Ask the board for a **pay rise** in the spring budget.
Try the AI on the **shop's stock orders**.
feel: Mildly **let down**, with the usual **money squeeze** underneath.
S0.quote: The cows still need milking at five, the mortgage still goes out on the first, and we're still two weeks from overdraft.
fieldNote: Tomas is already a **daily AI user** and sees the plateau as a small loss.
His **job feels safe** in a member-owned farm, but money is tight and stays tight.
He turns time saved into **family time**: a bedtime story instead of Sunday paperwork.

steps.text: Use AI for the milking rota, board reports and shop stock orders
Keep milking 120 cows on grass and ask for a spring pay rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's close to what I hoped for, actually. Most of the thinking jobs on our farm are paperwork I'd happily hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small farms and co-ops to catch up with the big players, if we share the tools. I'd say it at the co-op network meetings and post about what we're doing at Eastfield. And I'd say the gains should go to workers and members, not software companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me, mostly. The parts of my job that wear me out, the ordering and the reports, get done for me, and the parts I'm best at stay. The worry is that the board decides they don't need a full-time manager if the software plans everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the shop's ordering, the vet bookings and the milk recording onto AI tools within six months. I'd run a free evening session for other co-op farms in the region, maybe once a month. And I'd show the board that I'm the one making it work, so my job looks more valuable, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a little worry in the corner. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the board might not need a full-time manager. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very, I think. But one of the trustees, a retired accountant, already asks why we need two people on the vegetables. I'd keep an eye on that conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots spreading slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milking robot would come up sooner or later. A milking robot costs about the price of our house, so the members should vote on it, not whoever's on the board that year.

say: I'd say this helps **small farms and co-ops** catch up, if we share tools.
I'd say the gains should go to **workers and members**, not software firms.
think: I think it's mostly **good for me**: the ordering and reports go, the cow work stays.
The worry is the board deciding they don't need a **full-time manager**.
do: Move **ordering, vet bookings** and milk recording onto AI within six months.
Run a free **monthly evening session** for other co-op farms.
Show the board that he **makes the tools work**.
feel: **Excited**, with a small **worry** in the corner.

fieldNote: Tomas sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, because his day is mostly hands-on.

His progressive views show in wanting a **members' vote** on robots.
He notices one trustee who could **question staff costs**, a small but real worry.

steps.text: Move shop ordering, vet bookings and milk recording to AI tools

Learn the new milk-recording software inside six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fast, then. 2028 for the planning, 2031 for the hands. That would test everything we've built at Eastfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this is exactly why things like farms should be owned by communities, not funds. If the robots belong to members, the gains stay in the village. I'd also call for public money for co-ops to buy robots before the big companies buy all the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the planning side of my job is gone by 2028, the grazing, the orders, even the board reports. What's left is cows and people, and I'm good at both. By 2031, with robots, the question is whether 600 members want to pay a manager at all, and on two weeks' savings I can't afford to find out the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to make Eastfield the place that shows how a co-op runs with AGI, and get a grant for it. I'd ask the board for a three-year contract now, while I'm the one they need. And Ines and I would start putting fifty pounds a month aside, which hurts, but we'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but awake. I'd rather face it than hide from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between AGI and robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be useful in a new way. The AI does the thinking, but someone still milks, still calls the vet when a cow looks wrong, still talks to members. I'd use those three years to make that role so clear the board would keep it after the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't afford to find out the hard way. What does the hard way look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A board meeting in 2031 where they vote to buy the milking robots and cut the manager's post to part-time. My partner Ines's part-time teaching wouldn't cover the mortgage on the terrace. That's the picture that would wake me at three in the morning.

say: I'd say this is why farms should be **community-owned**, not owned by funds.
I'd call for **public money** so co-ops buy robots before big firms buy land.
think: I think the **planning side** of my job is gone by 2028.
By 2031 members may not want to **pay a manager** at all.
do: Bid for a **grant** to make Eastfield a model co-op farm with AGI.
Ask the board for a **three-year contract** while he's most needed.
Start saving **fifty pounds a month** with Ines.
feel: **Nervous but awake**, preferring to face it than hide.
S2.quote: My partner Ines's part-time teaching wouldn't cover the mortgage on the terrace.
fieldNote: Tomas expects his role could **shrink to part-time** around 2031, and that sets his mood.
He'd use the **three-year gap** to make the human role on the farm indispensable.
He still believes **community ownership** keeps the gains local.
His adaptability is real, but **thin savings** make him cautious about the hard way.

steps.text: Bid for a grant to run Eastfield as a model AGI co-op farm
Call for public money so co-ops can buy robots first
Save fifty pounds a month with Ines from now on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a planning horizon I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to put community farms and co-ops at the front of this, if government helps. I'd say it at the regional co-op network and in the local paper. I'd be loud about it being a choice who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to become the person every co-op farm in the region calls. AGI in 2031 takes the office work, robots in 2034 take some of the yard work. If I've spent the five years building a reputation, I've got options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short course in farm robotics, the kind the agricultural college runs in winter. I'd start a paid advice service for other co-op farms, maybe two days a month. And I'd get the members to start a robot fund now, so we buy our own when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. Nervous on the money, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ines say about the advice service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would say I already work too many hours, and she'd be right. But two days a month at two hundred pounds a day would double our savings in a year. She'd agree if I promised to stop the Sunday emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Freya and Leo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The machines will do lots of jobs. I'd tell my daughter Freya and my son Leo to be the people who decide what the machines are for. Freya would roll her eyes. Leo would ask if the robot can play football.

say: I'd say five years is time to put **co-ops at the front**, with government help.
I'd keep saying it's a **choice** who owns the robots.
think: I think five years lets me become the person **every co-op calls**.
With a **reputation** built, I'd have options when robots come in 2034.
do: Take the college's **winter course** in farm robotics.
Start a **paid advice service** for co-op farms, two days a month.
Get members to start a **robot fund** now.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter Freya and my son Leo to be the people who decide what the machines are for.
fieldNote: With five years, Tomas sees a **career path**, not just a threat.
His **advice service** idea would double their savings, and he's honest about the hours.
He keeps the **ownership question** front and centre, true to his progressive views.

steps.text: Take the agricultural college's winter course in farm robotics
Offer paid advice to co-op farms two days a month
Get members to start a co-op robot fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd be one of the people setting it up, not one it happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to make sure every rural community owns a piece of what's coming. I'd push for a national fund for community farm machines. And I'd say it again and again, because people forget fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable for me. By 2036 I'm fifty-three, the kids are nearly grown, and I'd have a decade of experience running AI on a working farm. The money worry doesn't go away, but my skills are worth more each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing everything I'm doing now with the tools, and add a robotics course in year two. I'd help write the co-op's ten-year plan with a robot budget in it. And I'd start paying a little extra off the mortgage, maybe thirty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Interested, even. The money's still thin, so not completely relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Eastfield you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mags, who's run the vegetable beds for fifteen years. She doesn't touch computers and she's nearly sixty. I'd want the co-op to make sure she retires on her terms, not the robot's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still keep you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies use the decade better than we do. The big companies have got lawyers and money and lobbyists, and we've got 600 members and a WhatsApp group.

I'd push for a **national fund** for community farm machines.
think: I think ten years is **manageable**, because my skills grow more valuable each year.
The **money worry** doesn't go away, even with time.

Write a **robot budget** into the co-op's ten-year plan.
Pay **thirty pounds a month** extra off the mortgage.
feel: Mostly **fine** and even **interested**, though not fully relaxed about money.
S4.quote: The big companies have got lawyers and money and lobbyists, and we've got 600 members and a WhatsApp group.
fieldNote: Tomas expects to **gain** from a slow transition, as a farm manager who already uses AI.
He worries for an older colleague, **Mags**, more than for himself.
His fear is that **big companies** use the decade better than co-ops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the board would be making big choices in a panic and I'd have no savings to ride it out. What would help is public money for co-ops to own their own robots, and a contract that gives me a few years of security while we work it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's in the room when the decisions get made. At Eastfield it's 600 members, which is messy but fair. Elsewhere it's one owner or one fund. On most farms, the people milking the cows never get a vote.

headlineQuote: On most farms, the people milking the cows never get a vote.
portrait: Tomas is the **farm manager** at a 600-member co-op dairy and vegetable farm.
He uses **AI every day** for grazing plans, rotas and board reports.
He has **two weeks** of savings, a mortgage, and a partner who teaches **part-time**.
He believes **community ownership** of robots keeps the gains local.
He stays **uneasy** in most scenarios, turning **anxious** when AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the board would decide **in a panic** with no savings to fall back on.
